🇮🇱 Israeli exit polls: Netanyahu loses majority, no one has a path to power

Exit polls from Israel's main broadcasters show a hung Knesset, with neither camp reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority.

Channel 12 gives Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc 52 seats, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 50, and the Arab parties a record 18. Kan and Channel 13 both project 53 for Eisenkot, 50 for Netanyahu and 17 for the Arab parties. Only the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 has his bloc at 60.

Netanyahu's camp is projected to collapse from 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset to 50. Yet Likud remains the largest single party with 24 to 25 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar at 21 to 23.

The surge in Arab representation is now the deciding factor. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out governing with Arab-led parties, which leaves Eisenkot's bloc short without them. If neither side can form a coalition, Israel heads to yet another election, with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.

Turnout hit a record high, and earlier in the day the electoral committee rejected Likud's request to keep polls open longer. Official results could take days.

📄 Iranian, Russian presidents pledge to expand bilateral ties, advance joint projects

📌 Moscow, IRNA – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin reaffirmed their commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation and advancing joint projects during talks in Moscow.

The two presidents met on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) to review bilateral relations, assess the progress of joint projects and discuss regional developments.
​
President Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its continued political, security and economic support, noting that bilateral trade was growing.
​
He said unilateral US actions underscored the need for stronger multilateralism and closer cooperation among countries facing sanctions.
​
He also stressed that regional states had the capacity and determination to resolve their challenges without relying on the United States.
​
The Iranian president said the two countries could expand cooperation in science, economics, industry, culture, security and defense. He highlighted cultural festivals held in Moscow, Kazan and Astrakhan and announced that Iran had issued the necessary permits for Russia’s state radio and television broadcaster to establish a representative office in Iran. He also welcomed plans for reciprocal cultural and media exhibitions in Tehran.
​
President Putin said trade between Russia and Iran had increased by 10.4 percent in the first eight months of 2026. He confirmed that construction of the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant was continuing and said Russia was fulfilling its commitments under joint projects with Iran.
​
The Russian president also expressed hope for positive developments in the Middle East and described the GECF summit as constructive. He said Russia was always pleased to host the Iranian president.

🚨 CALIFORNIA ELECTION BATTLE: THE DOJ LOSES AN EMERGENCY APPEAL — BUT THE LEGAL FIGHT IS FAR FROM OVER.

With just ONE WEEK remaining before the November 3 elections, the battle between California and the DOJ over more than 20,000 potentially ineligible registered voters has reached the Ninth Circuit.

Yesterday, a three-judge panel dismissed the DOJ’s emergency appeal in a 2–1 ruling.

Interestingly, TWO of those judges were Trump appointees.

But here’s what I believe people are missing:

THE NINTH CIRCUIT DID NOT SETTLE THE UNDERLYING LEGAL ARGUMENT.

The appeal was dismissed as premature because the district court had not yet ruled on the DOJ’s emergency request.

The case is NOT over. The underlying questions remain unresolved.

Trump-appointed Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, arguing that federal law prevents California from commingling ballots likely cast by noncitizens with legitimate ballots.

The majority raised concerns about federal intervention in an election already underway.

I’ve been arguing for months that many of these election-related confrontations may be part of a larger process of establishing the legal boundaries of federal authority BEFORE the November 3 elections.

And I believe this California confrontation may have been intended to reach federal court from the beginning.

Think about what we’ve been tracking:

• DOJ demands for state voter-registration records.

• Federal lawsuits challenging state election procedures.

• Supreme Court litigation involving mail-in ballots and election deadlines.

• Increasing federal involvement in election-security preparations.

• Repeated legal confrontations over the division of federal and state election authority.

What if the objective isn’t simply to win an individual emergency motion?

What if the larger objective is to force these disputes into the federal judiciary, where the questions can be formally adjudicated and potentially establish precedents governing future elections?

That’s the pattern I’ve been watching.

And yesterday’s ruling does NOT end that process.

In fact, the DOJ’s underlying request remains before federal Judge David O. Carter in Los Angeles.

Depending on what happens next, additional appeals could follow, potentially bringing substantive legal questions before higher courts.

But it is entirely reasonable to examine whether these successive legal battles are helping clarify the powers and limitations of the federal government when it comes to election integrity.

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

The immediate question is whether California can be required to segregate ballots associated with individuals suspected of being noncitizens.

The larger question is who ultimately has the authority to enforce federal election law when federal and state officials disagree.

And THAT question is still very much alive.

November 3 is only seven days away.

I don’t believe this confrontation is finished. I believe we’re watching another chapter in a much larger legal process.
